candidates.title: 7 Black Friday EDC knife picks that range from genuinely practical to delightfully unnecessary
candidates.full_text:
Every Black Friday I tell myself I’m shopping for other people, and every Black Friday a knife somehow ends up in my own pocket. This year I’m making it easier on all of us. WE Knife Co., the company behind WE Knife, CIVIVI, and SENCUT, is running its holiday sale with up to 30% off across all three brands (plus free gifts with purchases). I’ve picked seven knives from that lineup, ranging from a $40 award winner to a $185 titanium flagship. Whether you’re gifting or “gifting,” there’s something here for every pocket and every budget.

SENCUT holds down the entry level, CIVIVI covers the $60 to $100 sweet spot most of us actually carry, and WE sits up top with titanium, MagnaCut steel, and machining that borders on showing off. A brand-new CIVIVI Elite tier now splits the difference between those last two. The Elementum shows up twice on this list, once as a $65 CIVIVI and once as a $185 WE, which makes for a fun lesson in what extra money actually buys you. Three of these designs have BLADE Show awards to their name, so the list comes pre-vetted. Grab a coffee and maybe your wallet, because we’re going from fanciest to friendliest.

The WE Elementum takes CIVIVI’s best-selling silhouette and rebuilds it out of materials that would make a gear nerd weep a little. The blade is CPM MagnaCut, which makes this XA series the first WE knife ever to use the steel. MagnaCut was designed by metallurgist Larrin Thomas to solve an old trade-off, using niobium and vanadium carbides for edge-holding while keeping chromium free to fight rust. In plain English, it stays sharp, shrugs off sweat and humidity, and handles abuse without chipping. Here it’s cut into a 2.96-inch drop point with a flat grind and a black stonewashed finish, which hides scratches better than I hide my Amazon orders.

Bronze and black 6AL4V titanium forms the handle, delivering a lightweight, strong, and highly corrosion-resistant construction. WE machines the scales with a 3D topographic pattern inspired by geological layers, so the knife looks like a trail map while the ridges give your fingers some bite. That same titanium doubles as the frame lock, which clicks into place behind the blade after the flipper sends it out on caged ceramic bearings. The whole thing weighs 2.39 ounces (67.8g), about as much as three AA batteries, and closes to a pocket-friendly 4.02 inches (102.1mm). A reversible titanium clip means lefties get invited to the party too.

WE built its name on flippers and frame locks, so it was a fun plot twist when its Notchline hunting knife won Factory Imported Fixed Blade of the Year at BLADE Show 2026. The 3.45-inch (87.7mm) straight back blade is sized for field dressing, where control matters more than reach. It’s stonewashed CPM S35VN, a powder steel that holds an edge through a long day of skinning and still sharpens without a fight. At 0.17 inches (4.2mm) thick, the stout spine can work around joints, while the flat grind keeps cuts clean. Spine jimping gives your thumb a place to park when you choke up for detail work like caping.

Milled rose carbon fiber covers the full tang, machined with swirling, petal-like patterns that give your fingers real traction. The handle runs 4.05 inches (102.9mm) long and 0.71 inches (18mm) thick, chunky enough to fill your palm properly when your hands are cold or slick in the field. Everything weighs 3.98 ounces (112.8g), almost exactly a stick of butter, which feels appropriate for something this good at cutting. It rides in a black Kydex sheath with a T-Clip designed by knifemaker Bob Terzuola, so it mounts on a belt, a pack strap, or anything with webbing. A paracord lanyard tied through the tang makes it easier to draw from the sheath, even with gloves on.

Tilt the knife and you can steer the ball through the maze, exactly like those handheld puzzle toys from birthday party goodie bags. candidates.title: 125 Nm in a drop-bar bike is a different kind of fast
candidates.full_text:
Berria builds the Mistral Essential Apex around DJI’s Avinox M2 drive, the system family behind a new wave of electric mountain bikes, and sells it in road and gravel versions at €3,499 each. The motor numbers lead the story here.

Both versions share one hydroformed aluminum frame, one full carbon fork and one SRAM Apex XPLR build. A single choice separates them, and it sits at the contact patch, where a 40 mm gravel tire or a 32 mm road tire decides what the bike does best.

This article contains affiliate links, and Gadgeteer may earn a commission when readers buy through them.

Canyon Grail:ON CF 7 AXS Carbon gravel frame · Mid-drive electric assist · 12-speed drivetrain Price: $3,318.68 Where to buy: Buy on Amazon

Berria Mistral Essential Apex Gravel or Road version · Avinox M2 drive · 600 Wh battery Price: €3,499 Where to buy: Buy at Berria

The Avinox M2 is rated at 125 Nm of torque in Boost mode and 1,100 W of peak power, figures that belong to full-strength electric mountain bike drives rather than the lightweight systems usually tucked inside e-road frames. We covered this drive family in our Amflow TL Carbon first look , where the same Avinox hardware hauls a trail bike up climbs that would end a road ride early. Torque decides steep days. It governs how hard the motor twists the cranks at the low cadences where ramps and loose gravel slow a rider down, and 125 Nm is a great deal of twist when you’re pinned on a ramp.

The battery is an Avinox 600 Wh pack fixed inside the down tube, and that capacity is the generous half of the trade, feeding a full-power motor through full-length rides instead of rationing assistance on longer routes. The other half is weight. Berria leaves the weight of both versions off its spec sheet entirely, and that omission tells you this isn’t a bike you shoulder up three flights of stairs each night. A 600 Wh pack and a full-power motor add real mass regardless of how slim the frame looks in the photos, so riders who carry a bike daily should weigh the silence carefully.

Berria publishes no range figure for either version, a welcome restraint in a category addicted to optimistic laboratory numbers. The DPC100 display shows a live range estimate as you ride, next to cadence and your own power output, and that’s the number worth trusting.

Both versions ride on the same Mistral HPR 2G frame in hydroformed 6061 aluminum, with full internal cable routing, flat-mount brake calipers and clearance for tires up to 700x50c. Internal routing keeps the lines clean and the frame washable after muddy rides, and the 50c ceiling leaves room to grow the tires later.

The gravel version rolls on Vittoria Terreno T30 tires in 40-622, while the road version switches to Vittoria Rubino IV tires in 32-622 with the Graphene 2.0 compound, and both sit on Vision Team 30 alloy wheels. Five sizes run from 48 to 60. Every size wears the same BLACK-Collection finish, so the checkout choice really is just the tire question.

Shifting comes from a SRAM Apex XPLR D1 drivetrain with twelve speeds and a 10-44T cassette, braking comes from SRAM Apex hydraulic discs, and the Allroad EVO 3 fork is full carbon. That fork earns its keep on broken pavement, where carbon takes the buzz out of your hands across a long day, while the single chainring and wide cassette keep shifting simple on climbs.

The cockpit pairs an Avanforce alloy gravel bar with a carbon seatpost and a Selle Royal ORMA saddle. Up front, the Avinox DPC100 display packs a 2-inch color screen with Bluetooth and a USB-C port, so the bike can top up a phone while it reports your ride. The system also carries Bluetooth and Apple Find My, so a parked Mistral can be tracked from a phone like a misplaced set of keys. Nothing here is exotic.

Berria sells the Mistral through its European storefront in euros, and the charger in the box is a 230V unit fitted with an EU plug, so an American buyer is importing this bike rather than ordering it locally. None of that makes the bike worse. It does mean warranty trips, charger adapters and delivery timelines belong in the buying decision from the start, not in a forum post once the box lands.

Riders who want a comparable drop-bar e-gravel bike from a domestic storefront today can look at the Canyon Grail:ON CF 7 AXS, which Amazon carries at $3,318.68 with a carbon frame and mid-drive assist. It trades the Avinox punch for a domestic checkout and US support channels.

candidates.title: A Metal Cloud Frames the Desert Without Hiding It
candidates.full_text:
The desert is something that I really don’t want to visit, as someone who is not fond of arid or humid weather (although I live in a place that always has the latter). But I have to admit that it can really be picturesque and instagrammable, if you get the right angle or view. It is a landscape where you can have a lot of art installations and exhibits which can encourage people to actually pay a visit and make it a tourist attraction.

French artist Vincent Leroy has built a cloud with almost nothing to hide behind. Molecular Cloud Wireframe, a kinetic installation in Morocco’s Agafay Desert, outlines intersecting spheres with curved metal ribs. Instead of disappearing behind a solid object, you have the spaces between them letting the surrounding terrain to become part of the composition. Basically, you get a cloud that you can look through.

What this installation is trying to solve is how to put an object that will immediately grab people’s attention in an already striking landscape that you don’t need to reduce that to just scenery. A lot of the sculptures that we see sometimes dominate that scenario so what they wanted was a sculpture that needs a presence but not overwhelm it. Leroy’s open framework offers a persuasive answer. I like that it gives the eye a shape to follow while leaving room for everything around it. The desert isn’t being asked to step aside so a piece of art can have its moment since the former is the main character of course.

The name makes me picture a computer model before its surfaces have been added. That association appeals to me because the construction remains legible. You aren’t looking at a convincing imitation of a weather system. You’re being shown the lines that suggest one, with enough gaps for your brain to finish the job. To my mind, that’s more engaging than a literal cloud, however impressively someone might build it.

Light gives the framework another layer of variation. According to the project description, daylight emphasizes the depth of the overlapping spheres, while dusk turns the assembly into a flatter silhouette against the sky. A change in illumination alters how easily the eye can separate its parts. That seems a particularly fitting quality for an object borrowing its identity from something as changeable as a cloud.The wireframe version carries a recognizable geometry into a different material expression. It gives the familiar silhouette a much more exposed construction.

His background helps explain that interest in building an effect from relatively straightforward elements. Leroy studied industrial design in Paris and began producing kinetic works during his studies. His practice has since moved across sculptures, installations, and collaborations, with movement remaining central. I’m interested in that overlap between design and art: the technical arrangement matters, but the result doesn’t need to justify itself by making a household task easier or shaving seconds off a routine.

For the Coachella installation, Leroy described deliberately slowing movement to encourage a more contemplative experience. That’s an artistic intention, rather than a guaranteed response from everyone watching. Still, it offers a useful way to approach his work. I don’t need a sculpture to deliver a profound emotional reset. Giving me a reason to notice a changing shape for longer than a passing glance would be enough. Curiosity is a perfectly worthwhile outcome, especially when the underlying idea is easy to grasp.

Leroy has previously explained his relationship with technology, saying that it’s not the “end in itself” but he uses it as a a tool that “serves form, movement, emotion, and poetry.” That feels like a sensible standard for evaluating kinetic art. An elaborate mechanism can be fascinating, but technical complexity alone doesn’t make an object compelling. The movement has to contribute something to how we understand the form, or it risks becoming a demonstration looking for a purpose.

Molecular Cloud Wireframe gives me a clear reason to care about its form before needing a full engineering explanation. Its openness makes the setting indispensable to the idea. Move the same structure into a crowded exhibition hall, and I suspect its character would change considerably. Out in the desert, the gaps have somewhere to lead your eye. That’s the choice I appreciate most: Leroy has made an object with a recognizable outline while allowing the view beyond it to remain worth
